title: Britain's biggest explosion

facts.text: At 11:11 a.m. on Monday 27 November 1944, the underground bomb store at RAF Fauld in Staffordshire blew up. It is generally counted as the largest explosion ever on British soil.
RAF Fauld, No. 21 Maintenance Unit, kept the RAF's bombs in the tunnels of an old gypsum mine. About 4,000 tonnes of explosives went up, including some 3,500 tonnes of bombs.
The blast tore open a crater about 100 feet deep and roughly 300 yards across. It is still there, now called the Hanbury Crater, and still holds explosives.

Upper Castle Hayes Farm simply disappeared, farmhouse, people and animals. The blast also destroyed a reservoir, and its flood swept into the neighboring plaster works and mine, drowning many of the workers.
About 70 people died: RAF men, civilian workers, Italian prisoners of war who worked in the dump, the plaster workers and the people on the farm. Civilian deaths outnumbered military ones.
One of the RAF dead was Leading Aircraftman William Deuchars, 38, a painter from Crieff in Perthshire before the war. He is buried in Crieff Cemetery.
The explosion was heard in Birmingham and Coventry and registered on seismographs in Switzerland.

At first enemy action or sabotage by prisoners was suspected. The secret inquiry found the likely cause was a worker removing a detonator from a live bomb with a brass chisel instead of a wooden tool, and blamed staff shortages, inexperienced workers and pressure to work faster.
The report was not made public until 1974.

declassified.fact: The civilian dead of Fauld are named in the Civilian Roll of Honour kept in Westminster Abbey, a register of more than 67,000 names that Sir Fabian Ware had proposed to Churchill.

body:
Upper Castle Hayes Farm was there at 11:10 that morning. A minute later the farmhouse, its people and its animals were gone.

27 November 1944. The RAF's underground bomb store at Fauld in Staffordshire, in the tunnels of an old gypsum mine, blew up. About 4,000 tonnes of explosives went off, generally counted as the largest explosion ever on British soil. It was heard in Birmingham and Coventry, and a burst reservoir flooded the plaster works next door.

About 70 people died, among them Leading Aircraftman William Deuchars, 38, a painter from Crieff. The secret inquiry pointed to a worker taking a detonator out of a live bomb with a brass chisel. Its report stayed hidden until 1974.
